body.head: Theatrical Examiner.
body.p: Thursday evening produced another substitute for Mrs. Dickons (who is now possessed by the Lyceum Theatre) in the person of Miss Feron. With a voice of more power and compass, though of less science and correctness, than Mrs. Dickons, Miss Feron has greatly hurt her instrument by straining at imitations, which have procured her the cognomen of the English Catalani. She had better forego this ambition: there will never be but one Catalani: that divine singer's notes, loud and thrilling as they are, appear to come naturally from her miraculous organ: Miss Feron labours to pierce the ear; and she does pierce it, but then it is with pain. Her appearances at Covent Garden were very judiciously upon her own merits, as Miss Feron, the representative of Floretta, in Mr. Thomas Dibdin's trinket Opera of The Cabinet. In this part she has already appeared twice; but we are still unwilling to offer any thing like a settled judgment of her merits as a performer. The novelty of a new appearance,—the pleasure which it is impossible not to feel when any thing like female talent is met with on the Stage, and the natural prejudice in favour of youth and good looks and lively acting, are too strong not to embarrass the more sober judgment of criticism. But Miss Feron has, with all those allowances for a prejudice in her favour, very considerable merits. As a singer, her voice is uncommonly distinct and strong; she pronounces the words articulately, and accompanies her song with an action seldom inappropriate, and sometimes not ungraceful. Her acting is quick, lively, and natural. She seems made for coquettes and chamber-maids. Her pertness and vivacity were very amusing in Floretta, and some of her bye-play conveyed probably much more intelligence than the author had contemplated. If Miss Feron succeeds in this spirit, she will be an admirable acquisition to some of our Opera writers.

may be a work of supererogation in a Commentator, but in the present state of the Musical Drama, would be a most invaluable talent in an Actress; and we give Miss Feron the credit of making some of her part intelligible, and all of it amusing, beyond any possible intention of the Author. A figure like Miss Feron's is not made for the Heroines and Queens of the Stage: the sweeping robe, and sable pomp and haughty step of Mandanes and Elfridas, were not made for her; but as a representative of the light sportiveness and arch intrigue of the Comic Opera, we have seldom seen one who could contrive to put at once more meaning in her merriment, and more merriment in her meaning. The fault of her voice is a wildness which defies all the control of the Orchestra. Her acting is sometimes as unrestrained as her voice; but they both appear to have excellent materials for improvement, and we expect much pleasure from the corrected and polished taste which it should be her first labour to acquire.
